title: Social media sensationalism in the male infertility space: A mixed methodology analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 52 most-engaged male-infertility article links circulating on Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit and Twitter (Sep 2018-Aug 2019). Two reviewers graded each link accurate, misleading or inaccurate against the cited references and the peer-reviewed literature; 44% were misleading/inaccurate - a quantitative falsity share with an explicit denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language content; authors at UCLA, USA)
estimates.platform: Article links shared on Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit and Twitter (identified via BuzzSumo)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-engaged male-infertility article links graded misleading or inaccurate
estimates.value_raw: 44% misleading or inaccurate vs 56% accurate, of 52 article links (Table 1: 23 misleading/inaccurate vs 29 accurate); kappa=0.743
estimates.denominator: 52 unique article links about male infertility with the highest social-media engagement (from 8 search terms, each link with >=100 engagements; 421,004 total engagements)
estimates.definition: Link graded 'inaccurate' if the content was not supported by scientific literature, or 'misleading' if it mixed accurate and inaccurate information or extrapolated animal data to inappropriate conclusions about human fertility; the two categories are combined in the numerator
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Article links were classified as inaccurate if the content was not supported by scientific literature. Content was classified as misleading if it contained a combination of accurate and inaccurate information, or if it extrapolated animal data to make inappropriate conclusions about human fertility.'
estimates.source_quote: Fifty-six percent of articles were accurate and 44% misleading/inac-
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); the same finding in Results, p. 593
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two medical-student reviewers with curricular training in critical appraisal independently graded each link as accurate, misleading or inaccurate by checking the references cited against existing peer-reviewed literature; two senior urologists with fellowship training in male reproductive medicine, blinded to the reviewers' decisions, adjudicated all discordances. Inter-rater reliability Cohen's kappa = 0.743.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the social media analytics tool BuzzSumo ... to identify the most shared male infertility content from September 2018 through August 2019. BuzzSumo gathers data across the social media platforms Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit, and Twitter to generate a list of article links with the highest online engagement. ... Terms were further excluded if no associated article links generated sufficient engagement (100 or more engagements).
estimates.notes: source_quote is the Abstract sentence (it ends on a hyphenated line break, 'misleading/inac-|curate'); the Results section states the same figure as 'Overall, 56% of articles were graded as accurate and 44% as misleading or inaccurate (κ=0.743).', which the two-column text rendering splits across interleaved columns and so cannot be quoted as one contiguous span. borderline=true on the construct call. The denominator is 52 UNIQUE article links, each counted once, so the percentage is a share of items (CONTENT), not a share of shares/engagements; engagement only truncated the sample, exactly as 'most-viewed' truncation does elsewhere, hence denom_selection=curated. A SHARING/content_share reading is defensible because the frame is 'the most shared content', but nothing here is engagement-weighted (the paper reports separately that accurate and misleading links did not differ in engagement, p=0.805). Data window Sep 2018-Aug 2019; year coded 2019 (end of window). Country not stated: English-language web content sampled globally.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted (subgroup or non-falsity figures): accuracy split within alternative-media-hosted links only (57% accurate vs 43% misleading/inaccurate, n=28) and the by-source cells of Table 1 - source subgroups, not the paper's headline; '90% of these links were graded as misleading' among links reporting non-human-model studies (a subgroup share with an unclear denominator - the animal/insect-model link count is never stated, only that they drew 24% of total engagements); '24% of total engagements' from animal/insect-model links (an engagement share of a study-design category, not a falsity share); '26% [of the 15 cited studies] had sample sizes <100' and 'over 90% of male infertility content online comes from non-peer-reviewed sources' plus the source mix (alternative media 54%, news 37%, journals 8%, medical centres 2%) - source provenance, not veracity; '17 (50%) referenced the same two original research studies and captured twice as many engagements as the remaining 13 studies combined' - a near-concentration statement, but it is about cited studies, not users or sources, and it gives no clean conc_group_pct/conc_share_pct pair as R1 requires (the '50%' is the share of links, and 'twice as many' is not a stated share of engagement).

rob.design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods content analysis. Frame: BuzzSumo analytics across Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit and Twitter, Sep 2018-Aug 2019; 20 candidate search terms screened by two fellowship-trained urologists, 10 kept on total engagement (>=1,000), 8 surviving after link-level exclusions. 80 links identified, 73 after de-duplication, 21 excluded (2 expired, 10 with <100 engagements, 3 off-topic, 5 non-English, 1 podcast), 52 analysed. Grading by two independent medical-student reviewers against cited references and peer-reviewed literature, with blinded senior-urologist adjudication of discordances; Cohen's kappa = 0.743. No random sampling (engagement-truncated convenience frame), no weighting by engagement, single one-year window, English only; the authors note the assumption that engagement implies endorsement is unverified.
rob.item6_quote: Article links were classified as inaccurate if the content was not supported by scientific literature. Content was classified as misleading if it contained a combination of accurate and inaccurate information, or if it extrapolated animal data to make inappropriate conclusions about human fertility.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, 56% of articles were graded as accurate and 44% as misleading or inaccurate (κ=0.743).
